summary: Defines two SMTP service extensions. The first lets a client and server use the BDAT command to send large MIME messages efficiently, and the second builds on BDAT to send binary data. It is experimental and was replaced by RFC 3030.

eli5.summary: Normally email gets sent in small text lines. This lets big or odd files be sent in one go, as they are.

questions: what is the smtp bdat command
how to send binary mime over smtp
how does chunking work in smtp
subtitle: Send large emails and binary attachments without encoding overhead.

tldr.problem: SMTP and MIME systems are slow when sending large attachments because messages must be scanned for special byte sequences during sending and receiving, and binary data must be encoded in text-safe formats like base64, adding overhead.
tldr.mechanism: Two SMTP extensions: CHUNKING adds a BDAT command that breaks messages into chunks with explicit byte counts (no special-sequence scanning), and BINARYMIME allows unencoded binary data. Both use ESMTP negotiation to confirm support.
tldr.outcome: Large and binary messages send faster without encoding overhead, but the receiver must support BINARYMIME or the client must fall back to text-safe encoding. This RFC is experimental and was replaced by RFC 3030.

today: RFC 1830 is an Experimental protocol, superseded by RFC 3030. Sending large and binary email through SMTP is now standardized in a way that improves on this early proposal.

sections.title: The Problem with Large and Binary Mail
sections.content:
MIME enables email to carry many kinds of data beyond plain text, but the existing SMTP protocol has two inefficiencies. First, SMTP scans messages for the byte sequence CR LF . CR LF to detect the end of message, requiring scanning on both send and receive. For large messages, this scanning is costly. Second, binary objects must be encoded using base64 or quoted-printable, which adds 33 percent or more overhead to the data size. When Internet mail increasingly carries multimedia content, these inefficiencies compound.

RFC 1426 already defined an extension for 8-bit text (8BITMIME), allowing text with the high bit set. This RFC extends SMTP further with two complementary mechanisms: CHUNKING for efficient large-message transport with explicit byte counts, and BINARYMIME to send raw binary without encoding.
sections.eli5: SMTP has two problems with big files. It has to scan every piece looking for special markers that mean the end, which is slow. And binary stuff has to be encoded in safe text, which makes it bigger. These extensions let you just say the size and send it raw.

sections.title: The CHUNKING Extension and BDAT Command
sections.content:
The CHUNKING extension introduces a new SMTP verb, BDAT (binary data), as an alternative to the DATA command. A client indicates support by sending EHLO; if the server responds with the CHUNKING keyword, it supports the extension.

The BDAT command takes one required argument, the exact size of the data chunk in octets, and an optional LAST parameter. For example, BDAT 69 LAST tells the server the next 69 octets comprise the complete message. The server reads exactly that many octets, then returns a 250 response. This explicit byte counting eliminates the need to scan for end-of-message markers. For large messages, the client sends a series of BDAT commands, each with a size argument, followed immediately by that many data octets. Only the final BDAT carries the LAST parameter.

If the sender and receiver use ESMTP pipelining, they can stream multiple BDAT chunks. If an error occurs during transmission, the state becomes indeterminate and must be reset with RSET before further commands. DATA and BDAT cannot be mixed in the same transaction.
sections.eli5: Instead of scanning for the end of a message, you tell the server: here come 100 bytes. Then 200 more bytes. Then 50 more and that is all. The server counts and does not have to look for special markers.

sections.title: The BINARYMIME Extension
sections.content:
BINARYMIME extends SMTP to permit sending unencoded binary data without base64 or quoted-printable encoding. A client requests this by including BODY=BINARYMIME with the MAIL FROM command. The server responds with a 250 code to indicate it accepts binary MIME, or rejects the request if it does not support the extension.

BINARYMIME can only be used with CHUNKING and the BDAT command; it cannot be used with the standard DATA command. If a DATA command is issued after a MAIL FROM with BODY=BINARYMIME, the server should respond with error code 501.

The RFC notes that correct byte counting is critical: if too many bytes are indicated, the receiver waits for more data or misinterprets the next command as message data; if too few, the receiver interprets leftover data as invalid commands. Text in MIME messages sent as BINARYMIME must still be in canonical form with lines delimited by CR LF, even though no transformation of the message is performed during transmission.
sections.eli5: BINARYMIME says: send me the raw file bytes exactly as they are, no encoding. The server promises not to change a single bit. But only BDAT chunks can carry binary; the old DATA command cannot.

sections.title: Usage Examples
sections.content:
A simple CHUNKING example shows a client connecting to a server, sending EHLO, which returns the CHUNKING keyword. The client then sends MAIL FROM, RCPT TO, a single BDAT 69 LAST command with the message, and receives a 250 response.

A more complex example demonstrates pipelining with BINARYMIME. The client sends EHLO, the server responds with PIPELINING, BINARYMIME, and CHUNKING. The client then sends MAIL FROM addr BODY=BINARYMIME and multiple RCPT TO lines in a pipeline. The server responds to all of them at once. The client then sends two BDAT commands: BDAT 100000 (with 100,000 octets of binary MIME data), then BDAT 324 LAST (with the final 324 octets). The server confirms receipt of each chunk and the complete message.
sections.eli5: Simple example: ask if the server supports chunking, send a small message with BDAT 69 LAST. Complex example: ask for binary support, send the recipients at once, then send 100,000 bytes, then 324 more bytes marked as last.
